1Basic data

The record itself. The button above the panel steps through the five views; it is part of the page, never of a downloaded PNG.

2Luck versus toughness

Genera vs time: standing diversity through the whole record, data drawn solid and the model at the current luck dashed — blue for all living genera, red for those the small events are about to take. Slide luck until the red pair sits on top of each other.

Event Survival Curves: of those genera that reach to just before an event, the fraction that survive it, as a function of how long they had already existed.

Fractional Survival of genera alive at time t: of those genera, the fraction that exist just after an event.

Survivorship (Raup 1978, cohort analysis): subsequent survival probability of the genera that appear in one epoch, following the fraction still alive after each later extinction event; the bar marks the epoch the cohort was born into.

Technical analysis
Realizations10
ε0.050

Sweeps the luck factor 0–2.5 (step 0.1) and scores each value with the full-curve RMS fit error of ref. 1 (Methods C): event survival curves on the epoch-boundary grid, cohorts under 10 genera masked out, model value = median over realizations, residuals standardised by the Jeffreys binomial error added in quadrature to ε. Solid = event survival curves, dashed = fractional survival, dotted = Raup cohort survivorship. Ochre is the overall fit over all events and is always shown; the in-panel button adds a fit restricted to the events before 250 Mybp (red) or after 250 Mybp (blue). Changing ε is instant; more realizations are smoother but slower.

The MSD panel is the mean-square model–data gap of the three measures, averaged over many events; its in-panel button cycles between them. Below the fit-error sweep sit the three lifetime distributions: genus lifetimes, order mean lifetimes, and lifetimes normalised by each order's mean.

3Extinction–Origination

The Origination–Extinction matrix counts the genera that originate at one boundary and disappear at another — the data panel above, the model at the same luck below. Read along a row and you have one of Raup's survivorship curves; read down a column and you have the age structure of one extinction.

4Taxonomic Orders

Order diversity through time and the two 3D maps. Tap a cylinder in either map for its order or class. (The lifetime distributions have moved to Technical analysis in section 2.)

The Data/Model switch in the corner of each 3D map matters here. The model kills the right number of genera at every event but not the right ones, so it knows nothing of taxonomy: under Model, groups no longer die out as units and most classes run to the present. Trilobites end at the Permian in the data and survive it in the model — that gap is the point, not a fault.

Reading one group at a time

The transparency button under each map walks three steps — solid, 60% transparent, 85% transparent — so a crowded cube can be faded back until only the thing you are following stands out. The title of the map always says what is on show, from Orders, all phyla down to Order=Phacopida. On top of the transparency sit three nested spotlights:

Push a phylum and its cylinders go fully solid while everything else becomes completely transparent; the classes of that phylum then run down the left of both maps as a column of drawings. Push one of those drawings and that class alone stays solid — on the class map its own cylinder, on the order map every order belonging to it — while everything outside the class becomes completely transparent. Push a single order, either its cylinder in the order map or the picture under its description, and that order alone is solid: its sister orders in the same class drop to 85% transparent, so you can still see what it is being compared with, and every order in every other class disappears. The Order: … × chip lets go one level at a time, back to the class and then to the phylum.

Once an order is pushed the phylum is behind you: the context that is kept, named and drawn is the class, and the phylum buttons go back to All phyla. The left of both maps then carries the same three things stacked in the same order — the class's figures, the order's figures, and a picture of that order, its name in bold with the genus the drawing is of beneath it. Where the drawing belongs to that order it reads e.g.; where the class's drawing stands in for it, cf. On a short panel the picture is dropped before the figures are, and the class card shortens before either. The whole set of drawings is listed under Order silhouettes further down this column.

On a desktop, an order in the spotlight also brings up a small switch under the time rail, no wider than the rail itself and so lettered down its length. On Class the block carries every order of the class as a picture with its genus count written inside the lower left corner, the current one framed — the pictures are shrunk as far as they must be so that the whole class fits, however many orders it has. On Order only the one in the spotlight is drawn. Tapping any picture moves the spotlight sideways to that order, so a class can be walked through without going back to the cube. A phone or a tablet has no room for that block beside the cube, so there the stack is simply the two sets of figures and the one picture, and the switch is not offered.

The small ◂ Class 3D / ◂ Order 3D button in the corner of each map, just left of the Data/Model switch, hops straight between the two maps and keeps whatever is in the spotlight. Whatever is left fully solid is what a saved PNG is titled with — the order, class or phylum name in place of the panel's usual heading.

Silhouettes · what each drawing shows

Tap a cylinder in either 3D map and a small drawing of a representative member of that class appears under the info card; push a phylum instead and the whole column of its classes appears, and pushing one of those drawings puts that class in the spotlight. Every silhouette here was drawn for this applet as vector paths — original line art, nothing traced, photographed or copied, so there is no image licence to honour and nothing is fetched from the network. They are schematic and not to scale; the italic name is the genus the drawing is based on.

Provenance and rights. Every silhouette in this applet — the marine class and order drawings, and the land drawings of insects, arachnids, myriapods, dinosaurs, mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians — was drawn by Claude (Anthropic, model claude-opus-5) as original vector line art, written directly as bezier paths in the source of this file. None of them is traced, scanned, photographed, copied or derived from any photograph, museum specimen image, book plate or other existing artwork; the file embeds no image data and fetches nothing from the network, so every curve in it is arithmetic you can read in the source. They are therefore free of any third-party image rights and may be reused, modified and published with or without this applet. What the drawings depict — the animals, and the taxonomic and genus names that label them — are facts of natural history and carry no copyright of their own. They are schematic and not to scale: they are meant to identify a group at a glance, not to serve as reconstructions.

Data sources · and what the extra options do

Where the genera come from

Marine. J. J. Sepkoski Jr, A Compendium of Fossil Marine Animal Genera, Bulletins of American Paleontology 363 (2002), as analysed by M. Tikhonov et al., bioRxiv 2026-07. A curated list of marine genera with a first and last appearance for each, at stage and substage boundaries. It contains no land animals at all — every mammal in it went back into the sea.

Land. The Paleobiology Database (paleobiodb.org), an open compilation maintained by an international community and housed at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Downloaded from the occs/taxa endpoint with envtype=terrestrial (which covers fluvial, lacustrine, karst, eolian, cave and glacial settings) and taxon_status=accepted, so junior synonyms are not counted twice. Unlike Sepkoski's compendium this is an occurrence database: a genus's range here is the span of the intervals it has been collected from, so it is a measurement of the fossil record rather than an expert's judgement of the taxon.

Please cite both databases, not this applet, if you use the numbers.

How the land file was built

Only genus-rank records are kept. Plants, algae, protists and fungi are removed, as are ichnogenera — trace fossils are not taxa and must not be counted as genera. A few dozen records with Precambrian or essentially unconstrained first appearances are dropped: one ran from 1800 to 5 Ma, which is not a measurement. Some orders are re-filed, because PBDB's class field is phylogenetic and defaults up the tree: tetrapods come back labelled Osteichthyes and birds labelled Reptilia. Ages are snapped onto the boundaries the marine compendium already uses, within a tolerance that scales with age (about 1.5 Myr at 20 Ma, 9 Myr at 300 Ma), so that the two records share one event timeline.

Do the two records share their boundaries?

Largely, yes — and the applet measures it rather than assuming it. The marine compendium uses 84 extinction horizons; the land file uses 110. About 80% of the land genera (22,700 of 28,400) make their last appearance on a horizon the marine record also uses, which is why the two can be laid on one timeline at all.

The 43 land horizons with no marine counterpart are not disagreements; they are subdivisions. Every one of them lies between 0.01 and about 4 Myr from the nearest marine boundary, and almost all are Cenozoic: 13.8, 41.0, 45.9, 57.5, 21.5, 18.5, 7.1, 5.3, 3.6 and 1.8 Ma, plus two in the late Palaeozoic near 300 and 307 Ma. Land mammal ages slice the Neogene much more finely than a stage-level marine compendium can, so the land record simply carries horizons the sea has no name for. The reverse also happens at the other end: the marine record reaches back to 545 Ma, the land record only to 470 Ma.

This matters for one thing in particular. An extinction fraction pooled over both records divides by whatever was alive in both, so at a horizon only one record uses, the ratio is being taken against a denominator the other record never contributed to. That is what the Extinction counts panel is for: it plots raw last-appearance numbers, marine in blue and land in orange, and takes no ratio at all. A horizon used by only one of the two records shows there as a single bar standing alone. It appears as the first panel under Basic data, and only while Marine+Land is selected — with one record on screen there is nothing to compare. Its own switch toggles a logarithmic or linear count axis; log is the default, because the marine Palaeozoic and the land Cenozoic differ by two orders of magnitude.

The three record buttons

Marine, Land and Marine+Land choose which compilation is in front of you. In the combined view the marine order codes keep their own numbering and the land codes sit past them, so neither list is renumbered and a class that occurs in both — Gastropoda, Bivalvia, Mammalia — is a single class holding both sets of orders.

Aquatic groups appears whenever land genera are shown. The land file is a record of continental animals, which is not quite the same thing as land animals: freshwater fish, unionid bivalves, ostracods, eurypterids and the secondarily aquatic tetrapods (whales, sirenians, plesiosaurs, ichthyosaurs) all come out of non-marine deposits. About 8% of the genera carry that flag, and this button leaves them out. If a result depends on whether they are in or out, that is worth knowing.

No recent / With recent works on both records. Sepkoski ships two separate compilations; the land file is one file including the extant genera, so on land “No recent” simply drops the genera whose last appearance is zero. It is the same intent, not the same operation.

A caution about the land curve

The largest apparent extinctions in the land record fall at about 93 and 34 Ma, not at the Permo-Triassic or the K–Pg. Insects are 45% of the file, and those two horizons are where exceptional insect preservation begins and ends. What the curve is partly showing is the coming and going of Lagerstätten, not the death of animals. This is the reason Sepkoski restricted himself to the sea, and it is why the Aquatic groups switch and the phylum buttons are worth using before drawing a conclusion: if an event survives being restricted to tetrapods alone, it is far more likely to be real.

About this applet · abstract & references

In the fossil record it is the old who survive. A genus that has already weathered many an extinction is the more likely to weather the next, while the young perish easily. Must we then suppose that lineages grow hardier as they age? Using the Sepkoski marine genus compendium, this applet follows ref. 1 and asks the question the other way about: what if nothing in a genus ever changes, and the old merely appear sturdy because the frail were long ago swept away? That single idea — survivorship bias — with a single fitted parameter, reproduces the whole set of age-conditioned survival probabilities, the way extinction risk falls with genus age, and the distribution of genus lifetimes. The verdict is that Luck weighs a little heavier than intrinsic properties in the game of species survival. And Luck is here no idle word: it carries the fact that no two catastrophes are alike — one may be the ecosystem stumbling over its own feet (ref. 5), another the work of volcanoes, or of a stone that fell out of the sky.

The applet also lets the story be told a little differently, by giving every genus in a taxonomic order the same intrinsic toughness — as though fortune were dealt out by family rather than by individual. That toughness may be drawn at random; or it may be set in proportion to the average lifetime of the genera within the order, which is the more careful telling, for it lets kin meet the stresses of history together, as in truth they did. Fitted in that manner Luck grows more modest than intrinsic toughness: the best fit falls to 0.9, where before it stood at 1.5.

The applet opens the door to the orders themselves, to their diversity and their robustness (ref. 4). Among these views stands the Origination–Extinction matrix, which is, by its very construction, the whole family of Raup's (1978) survivorship curves gathered into a single picture — the same curves that were integrated along the extinction times in each of the survivorship curves of the analyses above.

Finally the applet opens for analyzing taxonomic classes in terms of the orders that they consist of, giving a bird's eye view on evolutionary relationships.
